## Function

CD86 is displayed by antigen-presenting cells and binds **CD28** to support T-cell co-stimulation and **CTLA-4** to help restrain responses. Its meaning depends on timing, receptor availability, and the activation state of both cells.

::: {.gene-mechanism}
::: {.gene-state}
**CD86 available**

Antigen recognition receives a context signal that can support or regulate T-cell activation.
:::
::: {.gene-flow-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.gene-state .gene-state-off}
**CD86 reduced**

T-cell priming may weaken, but inflammatory output can also change because CTLA-4 engagement is lost.
:::
:::

The UC hypomethylation signal is biologically compatible with abundant/activated antigen-presenting cells, but does not prove CD86 overexpression. Bulk biopsy composition is a major competing explanation.

## What the evidence adds

CD86 is not simply an “on” switch. CD28 and CTLA-4 share CD80/CD86 ligands but drive different outcomes, and B7-2/CD86 tends to appear early during antigen-presenting-cell activation [@sharpe2002b7]. More recent cell-biological work shows that CTLA-4 can physically remove CD86 from neighboring cells by transendocytosis; defects in that process can contribute to autoimmunity [@kennedy2022cd86]. A biopsy methylation value therefore sits several regulatory steps upstream of the biologically relevant quantity: receptor engagement at an APC–T-cell contact.

## Biomarker interpretation

A useful CD86 result would distinguish within-cell epigenetic change from recruitment of CD86-positive dendritic cells, monocytes, or B cells. Paired single-cell or spatial expression, immune-cell proportions, and protein localization would make a bulk DMR interpretable. Until then, CD86 hypomethylation is best described as an immune-state candidate marker, not evidence of net CD28 or CTLA-4 signaling.

<details><summary><strong>Best paired measurements</strong></summary>

Cell-type-resolved methylation, CD86 RNA/protein, APC abundance, CD28/CTLA-4 context, and tissue inflammatory state.
</details>
